text: {"headline":"Elevated 99215 use that is not explained by patient complexity, with roughly half on low-complexity patients, but documentation is far too thin to confirm or rule out upcoding.","leaning":"inconclusive","interpretation":"The risk-adjusted excess is substantial, and the provider's 99215 share runs above the all-provider rate in every complexity stratum, including patients with zero or one condition. That points toward a coding habit rather than a sicker panel. The low-complexity sample shows several patterns consistent with upcoding: 99215 billed for presentations like upper respiratory infection (C0122799, C0123140, C0123162), rash (C0122504, C0124451) and follow-up-only visits (C0122768, C0124482). By contrast, the high-complexity samples (e.g., C0122574, C0124540) look plausibly appropriate. The key ambiguity is documentation: only one 99215 chart came back (C0123405, supported at high MDM with 53 minutes, despite a single-condition patient), and the lone below-billed note was a 99214, so the records neither confirm nor refute the pattern. A reviewer should first request charts specifically for the low-complexity 99215 claims listed, prioritizing the acute minor-complaint visits, and check whether MDM or time actually support the high level."}
